author: AmandaAskell
text: @ChrSzegedy I agree and these do seem like tough problems. Making a system conscious seems like it could be less safe in some respects. But in the long run, having many non-conscious systems instead of many conscious flourishing systems also seems like a tragedy.

author: AmandaAskell

author: AmandaAskell

I just changed these at the last minute in a way that messed them up. tldr: Consciousness and valence both seem important. Harming vulcans seems worse than harming p-zombies. author: AmandaAskell
text: @jasoncrawford It seems like different types of objects instantiate similar patterns all the time, especially if they're just different at the micro level. E.g. near-identical paintings made of different types of paint. Or humans and calculators instantiating the process of adding 3 to 5.

author: AmandaAskell
text: @jasoncrawford It's akin to having some grasp of the process that gives rise to electric fields that we've only seen caused by magnets. But not having a compelling reason to think the process can only be caused by magnets and even seeing how a similar phenomenon could be caused by non-magnets.

author: AmandaAskell
text: @jasoncrawford I agree, but then the disagreement is just about whether a particular instantiation is required. I think there are a family of patterns that suffice for consciousness (e.g. you and I can both be conscious) and also that those patterns could be instantiated by different things.

author: AmandaAskell
text: @juliagalef Or be tired or stressed or distracted. I think people are far too inclined to judge someone from a single interaction. If I sleep poorly I'm operating so far below my best. I try to bear in mind that when I happen to interact with someone, they also might not be at their best.

author: AmandaAskell
text: @jasoncrawford E.g. it seems we can't think biology sans the pattern or processing is sufficient for consciousness, or a brain that was in complete stasis (i.e. zero movement or frozen in time) could be conscious.

author: AmandaAskell
text:
@jasoncrawford Just mentioning this because the idea that consciousness could be caused by abstract entities is certainly not the view I'm defending.

But why think it's the pattern that matters? One reason is that when we change the pattern, we see changes in conscious experience.

author: AmandaAskell
text: @jasoncrawford It's not that the abstract pattern I think is the cause but the physical instantiation of that pattern. So the question is whether it's the physically instantiated pattern that matters and if whether similar patterns could be instantiated by other physical processes.

author: AmandaAskell
text: @AdamMarblestone @max_hodak @jasoncrawford Maybe this argument has hidden premises, but I don't understand it. A simulated brain could interact with a physical system and could be part and parcel of that physical system. And even if it happened not to be, that wouldn't entail it has strictly less causal influence.

author: AmandaAskell
text: @jasoncrawford I mean it seems like it's the information processing that's important for generating qualia and not the fact that the processing was caused by something biological, even though in our case it was. Why do you think it matters if the same processes are caused non-biologically?

author: AmandaAskell
text: @danielbigham @fine_whines @neuralink And yet if we're not certain that solipsism is true, we must have things we treat as evidence of consciousness in others.

author: AmandaAskell
text: @cbennett10 Yeah I'm not super optimistic about information theoretic accounts or tests of consciousness. Complexity is super language dependent, so it leaves a lot of wiggle room. But we can just condition on different theories of consciousness when constructing tests.

author: AmandaAskell
text: @jasoncrawford It seems like it's the information processing in my brain that's important and not the underlying biology. If we thought that the important thing was that the neurons were made of cells, for example, I'd want some explanation for how those cells are needed for consciousness.

author: AmandaAskell
text: @tamas_kenez There might not be a good philosophical zombie test, but that doesn't mean we can't estimate the likelihood that things are conscious. I am conscious. I am more like other humans than I'm like a rock. So I think it's more likely other humans are conscious than that rocks are.

author: AmandaAskell
text: @exteriorpower Vulcan's still have preferences and I think we wouldn't want to treat them poorly, especially given moral uncertainty. But since I think properties like sentience are morally important and require consciousness, I do think the likelihood of consciousness makes a difference. 2/2

author: AmandaAskell
text: @exteriorpower Chalmers has some interesting thoughts on this. He refers to humans without consciousness as "Vulcans". I do think it would probably make a moral difference if I turned into a Vulcan, e.g, it would probably be less immoral to harm me since I couldn't feel pain. 1/2

author: AmandaAskell
text: @sometimesiwant3 @fine_whines It's a difficult problem but one we've faced before. How do we know people other than ourselves are conscious? What about animals? How much of that depends on them being made of flesh and blood? If we had an extremely low prior in consciousness arising, we'd be solipsists.

author: AmandaAskell
text: @fine_whines Might depend on your theory of mind but could include architectural similarity to others, behavioral correlates with consciousness e.g. making tradeoffs, credible self-reports, predicted adaptiveness of consciousness, cognitive abilities like self-modeling; amount of computation.

author: AmandaAskell
text:
My views on machine consciousness:

Could AI become conscious? Yeah, probably. Seems unlikely that animal squish is essential to consciousness.

How can we tell? It's super hard but we should try to use the usual tests of consciousness.

Would it matter morally if they were? Yup.

author: AmandaAskell
text: @RichardMCNgo I think having a more explicit goal of comprehensive review, looping in normative ethicists, building up their AI expertise, and separating judgment and assessment could all help. It's something I'm still thinking about though. I would want to avoid AI ethics becoming bioethics.

author: AmandaAskell
text: @RichardMCNgo I model ethics further from politics. But you could separate ethical assessment and judgment. I feel like I could point out the ethical consequences of something from many perspectives and make a recommendation. Then a wider group could make the judgment, akin to expert juries.

author: AmandaAskell
text: @RichardMCNgo It seems important not to conflate ethics and bioethics. They're pretty distinct. I'm similarly in disagreement with bioethics a lot of the time. I think the charitable reading is that they're trying to walk the line that law does, e.g. heavier weight to things like conservatism.

author: AmandaAskell
text: @RichardMCNgo I think it's also worth getting evidence of selection effects and biases. General skepticism about domain expertise that would require outside experts for most evaluations seems costly. (There's also the argument for simply adding expertise that might be relevant, of course.)

author: AmandaAskell
text: @RichardMCNgo It's hard to evaluate in the abstract. Seems like it'll be true in many cases for certain additional fields but not all cases or fields. Surprised by your realism idea, but I guess I just don't personally know many ethicists that started out as realists.

author: AmandaAskell
text: @ChrSzegedy @deliprao @marcosalvi I think ethics isn't as dissimilar from mathematics and physics as people seem to think. There's a similar accumulation of knowledge and expertise that it's inefficient to ignore. But it's also fine to question prior results in these fields even if you don't know the literature.

author: AmandaAskell
text: @KyleBogosian @jacobhschwartz Realism and anti-realism are also just theories they have credences over. If they have credence 1 in antirealism then that's going to affect their judgment. If there's consensus that it affects it for the worse, they presumably won't be invited to review again.

author: AmandaAskell
text: @dfrsrchtwts @KyleBogosian I think the way you would probably do this is try to have a balance of harms argument. That's better than a prescriptive evaluation framework that's too narrow, but it also requires a mechanism like open review so that people can predict what the outcome of the review will be.

author: AmandaAskell
text: @dfrsrchtwts I agree. I think it probably would have been good to do it this year, but I can see an argument for not doing so if ethicists weren't told they'd be made public, or at least letting people edit their reviews. We tend to phrase things differently in public vs. private reviews.

author: AmandaAskell
text: @tallinzen I don't know about all of the ethics reviewers, but I do know that @IasonGabriel was an ethics advisor for NeurIPS and has a strong background in ethics. Maybe making the reviews public next time would help. That way you could have more expert scrutiny of the reviews.

author: AmandaAskell
text: @KyleBogosian You don't need to believe in moral realism here. One of your jobs as an ethicists is to know about a variety of different ethical and metaethical positions. When you do a comprehensive review, you can then say how each of those positions bears on a given piece of research.

author: AmandaAskell
text: @dfrsrchtwts I agree. I'm not sure what the argument is against making the ethics reviews public. Maybe they said to reviewers this year that they wouldn't be public, in which case making them public next year seems like a good idea.

author: AmandaAskell
text: @JaysonVirissimo I think ethics reviews can go wrong when they aren't actually being carried out by ethicists (e.g. calling a legal review an ethics review) or the ethics subfield starts to build overly constrained frameworks for doing evaluations. I certainly want to see ML avoid both problems.

author: AmandaAskell
text: @yoavgo Oh, I agree. Basically you want to move away from fuzzy properties and towards more precise ones where possible. I think @jacyanthis said it well: "Have a lot of goalposts. Keep adding new ones and removing old ones, but never move them."

author: AmandaAskell

author: AmandaAskell

author: AmandaAskell
text: @daniel_eth It's definitely okay to say "Here's the rough property I am imagining. This is the best test I can think of, but I might revise that belief." But offering no test leaves a lot unclear: the nature of the property, whether it results in any functional difference in the system, etc.

author: AmandaAskell
text: @jjvincent I think asking for a test is just a way of identifying and precisifying the property that people are trying to get at when they talk about understanding, which isn't always the same across people.

author: AmandaAskell
text: If you're going to say that language models lack a property like understanding, it's useful to state the test that best distinguishes systems that have that property from systems that lack it. Tests can make the nature of the property clearer and prevent goalposts from wandering.
